messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Vinh's Vigil

Vinh Nguyen was sixty-eight when the bomb went off outside the community center in Minneapolis where he was conducting intake interviews for a resettlement program. He had spent forty-three years building a life in America after fleeing Saigon, and the last twelve of those years had been dedicated to helping others escape the places that had made him a refugee. On that Tuesday in March, he was sitting at a folding table with a young Syrian family, reviewing their documentation, when the blast shattered the front windows and toppled the metal shelving unit behind him. The explosion was not tremendously close—the device had been placed in a vehicle parked across the street—but the force was enough to throw him sideways, to fill the room with a sound like the world tearing open, and to coat everything, including his face and hands, with a fine gray dust that he would later learn was pulverized concrete and drywall.

The investigation determined it was a hate crime. The bomber was never caught. Vinh survived without serious physical injury, though he had sustained a mild concussion and multiple lacerations. The family he had been interviewing was not harmed. But something in the architecture of his mind had fractured in that moment—a rupture that widened in the weeks that followed.

Within days, Vinh had come to believe that he was responsible. Not for the bombing itself, but for having been there, for having continued his work, for having invited that family to that building on that particular morning. He had come to believe that his presence somehow drew danger, that his decision to return to the office instead of working from home that week had been reckless, that if he had only rescheduled the appointment by a single day, the bomb would have detonated to an empty street. This reasoning was circular and self-defeating, but it had taken root with the certainty of conviction. Vinh found himself replaying the morning in obsessive detail—the moment he chose his shirt, the route he drove, the exact time he arrived—each time identifying some choice he might have made differently, some small decision that might have altered the trajectory of events. The rumination became a kind of penance, as if by exhaustively cataloging his mistakes he might retroactively undo them.

He stopped driving. The thought of sitting in traffic, of being confined in a vehicle with no control over what might happen around him, became intolerable. His wife, Margaret, drove him to work, but even being a passenger filled him with a low-grade dread. He sat with his hand on the door handle, tracking the position of other vehicles, monitoring the distance between them and the car. After two weeks of this, he asked Margaret to drop him at a café three blocks from the office, and he walked the rest of the way, moving quickly along streets he had known for decades but no longer recognized as safe.

The office itself had been cleaned and repaired, but Vinh found that he could only work in the back room, away from the windows. He moved his desk to face the door so that he could see anyone approaching. His supervisor, noting the change, had asked if he wanted to take leave. Vinh refused. Taking leave felt like surrender, like allowing the bombing to claim more of his life than it already had. But the truth was that his productivity had collapsed. He was conducting fewer interviews, missing deadlines, and his colleagues had begun to notice his jumpiness—the way he would startle violently when someone knocked on the door, the way his hand would shake as he filled out forms. One afternoon, a colleague dropped a stack of metal trays in the break room, and Vinh found himself on his feet, heart hammering, unable to breathe normally for several minutes afterward.

At home, he had begun to avoid any conversation that might lead to disagreement. When Margaret suggested he speak to someone, a therapist or a doctor, he deflected. When his daughter called from Portland and asked if he was managing, he said yes, he was fine, though his voice carried a flatness she had never heard before. He could not bear the thought of conflict, of anyone questioning his narrative of blame or suggesting that he might not have been responsible. To argue would be to risk being told something he could not accept—that the bombing was not his fault—and that possibility terrified him more than the memory itself.

The memory was strange and fractured. Sometimes it played as a sequence of images: the woman's face across the table, the window exploding inward, the dust hanging in the air like a fog. Other times it was purely auditory—a high, sustained ringing in his ears, the sound of breaking glass repeated over and over, voices shouting words he could not quite make out. The visual and sonic elements did not always align. He would be lying in bed at night, and suddenly he would hear the blast again, so vividly that he would sit up in panic, only to realize that Margaret was asleep beside him and the house was silent. The memory felt unreal in a way that troubled him. Surely something so vivid, so sensorily overwhelming, must be accurate, must be the truth of what happened. Yet the very intensity of it made him doubt. Had it really been so loud? Had the dust really hung in the air for so long? The uncertainty gnawed at him. If he could not trust his own recollection, what could he trust?

Now, at seventy-two, Vinh had come to live in a very small world. He felt safe only in the back room of the office and in his bedroom at home. Everywhere else—the grocery store, the pharmacy, Margaret's book club when she insisted he attend—felt like walking through a minefield. He was hyperalert, scanning for threats, noting exits, calculating distances. A car backfiring on the street would send him rigid. A siren in the distance would make his stomach clench. He had not attended his granddaughter's school play because the auditorium felt too exposed, too full of people, too unpredictable. Margaret had wept when he told her he could not go.

What finally brought him to seek help was not his own recognition that something was wrong, but a quiet intervention by his daughter, who had driven down from Portland and sat with him in the back room of his office, and told him that she was frightened—not of the bombing, but of losing him to whatever this was that had taken hold of him since. She said she needed her father back. She said that she could not watch him disappear into this smaller and smaller space. Vinh had wept, and in that moment, something shifted. He was not certain he could be helped. He was not certain that he deserved to be. But he had made an appointment with a trauma specialist, and he had shown up, and he was sitting in a therapist's office for the first time in his life, trying to find words for a fear that had no name and a guilt that felt more real than anything else he knew.
